item.title: If It Looks Like a Duck, Swims Like a Duck, and Quacks Like a Duck, It's Probably a Shapeshifting Living Nightmare: So I just stumbled over this hidden gem
item.content:encoded:
It's 2020-12-19 and I technically came looking for something entirely unrelated, but upon the search spewing out this, I had to read it solely for the title. I was not disappointed.
It is kinda uplifiting to see such an (comparatively) old piece of the site still able to entertain 4 and a half years later even thought I perhaps only get a third of the references.

Whereas the first comment claims this reminds them of Terry Pratchchet, I would rather compare it to Douglas Adams. Which is quite a praise from someone like me.

I came looking for hacky CSS, expected Eldritch Horrors and found true happiness. Or something like that.

item.title: SCP-5129: Re: Picture
item.content:encoded:
So first off the picture needs to be at the top.

As noted by Karablue9482, there's no requirement for the image to always be at the top of the page. It's considered standard formatting for that to be the placement, but it's not necessarily the only location an image can be in an article.

item.title: SCP-5129: Picture
item.content:encoded:
So first off the picture needs to be at the top. In order to do this you need to go to files section (next to discuss) and upload the picture from your device. From there you need to put in the following code above item and containment class.

[[include component:image-block | name=Insert name of file here | caption=insert caption | width=WIDTH-GOES-HERE]

Additionally the image seems pretty unrealistic to me, was this made on roblox? You need to have the image as realistic as possible otherwise it may un-immere readers.

Hope this helps :)

item.title: SCP-5129:
item.content:encoded:
So it looks like this article is heading into the deletion range. I know that can often feel baffling or upsetting for a first time writer (trust me, you get used to it!), so please take this feedback as advice on your next SCP! If feedback seems harsh, it’s only because I hate when authors keep making the same mistakes until they give up on the wiki. Keep trying, you’ll get there!

Here are a few pitfalls you fell into:

SCP’s are written in clinical, precise language. This piece reads like prose, when a SCP should read like a formal scientific document. I strongly recommend reading the Clinical Tone Guide. Here are a few examples.

“a small table all the way in the back of the chamber”

“All the way in the back” is a very casual way of describing something. “Small” is imprecise.

“Whatever the wearer believes becomes real, and that's anything. Even accidentally.”

Sentence fragments used for emphasis can work in traditional prose, but are out of place in formal scientific writing.

“SCP-5129 seems to be rather “squared”, as if it was what could only be described as “8-bit”.”

“Seems to be” isn’t a great way to describe a SCP. The fictional reader isn’t interested in what it seems to be, they want to know what it is and what it looks like. If there’s a difference between what it is and what it looks like, that should be clear. Using “rather” is imprecise as well.

Beyond the writing style, the content of the SCP has some more fundamental issues. For one, your containment procedures are pretty overblown. From what I can tell, the glasses are only dangerous if somebody touches them. That makes them about as dangerous as a sample of smallpox or a piece of uranium, which is to say, Safe. Euclid is for objects that are unpredictable and need active containment, whereas this thing is fine as long as you don’t poke it. Lock it in a very secure box and don’t let anybody touch it. If you want to be extremely careful, maybe embed it in a block of plastic first. Bam, done.

There’s no narrative arc or story to this piece. Another commenter addressed this above, but basically, you’ve given us this interesting object that can cause all sorts of mayhem and a few lines of mystery about where it came from, but you haven’t gone anywhere with either premise. It’s all setup, with no conclusion.

Mystery and ambiguity is good, but it should be the sort of thing that leaves the reader asking questions once the story is complete. This piece asks the reader to construct a story purely in their head, but is too vague and open-ended to give us the momentum to get there. The payoff to a story can be a sense of horror or mystery, but it still has to be a payoff.

Hope at least some of this helps. I look forward to reading your next article! The wiki has a pretty high attrition rate, so don’t be too discouraged if it takes a while to get one to stick.

item.title: SCP-5129: Re: Almost Ideal
item.content:encoded:
These would be a pretty clear-cut Safe object- lock them in a box and never open it again, nothing bad will happen.

I like to point to SCP-2948 as the ultimate "dangerous safe" object- it's a literal nuclear bomb with unlimited yield… but it's safe because they've disabled the countdown timer and put it in a very sturdy box.
